one_line_concept: The last clerk of a closing county Hall of Records stamps, files, and surrenders the final deeds of a vanishing town, and every certificate becomes a collectible artifact of a place that no longer keeps its own memory.
visual_law: Every frame is shot dead-on or from a low clerk's-eye angle inside a records room: floor-to-ceiling index drawers, ledger spines, and a single brass-railed counter. The world is always indoors, always pre-digital municipal architecture (oak, frosted glass, linoleum, fluorescent tube light), and the hero object is always a document being processed, never a person performing. Composition is bilateral and bureaucratically symmetrical: the rubber stamp lands center-frame.
character_system: THE CLERK is faceless by design: a synthetic figure rendered only as hands, sleeve-gartered forearms, a grey cardigan, and the back or crown of a head bent over the counter. Identity is carried by recurring uniform signatures (ink-stained right index finger, a single brass key on a ball-chain, half-moon reading glasses set down, never worn). The Clerk is whoever holds the stamp. This lets any AI generation hold consistency through wardrobe and props, never a face, and lets the IP outlive any single render.
environment_system: A single closing institution, THE DEED OFFICE, explored room by room as a serialized world: the Counter (intake), the Stacks (index drawers A-Z), the Vault (sealed master ledgers), the Burn Room (deaccessioned records), the Window (where the public used to come). Each chapter is one room. Constrained, repeatable, archive-deep instead of location-random.
color_law: World is desaturated municipal grey-green and oak-brown, near-monochrome. ONE saturated color is permitted: STAMP-PAD VERMILION. Red appears only as wet ink: the stamp impression, the FILED mark, the deed seal, the wax. Red = officially recorded, made real, no longer reversible. Nothing else in the frame is allowed to be red.
symbol_system: A round government stamp impression: a single ink circle with a horizontal line across its middle (the date slot). Five seconds to draw: draw a circle, draw one line through it. That circle-with-a-bar is the DEED OFFICE seal, the logo, the watermark, and the literal product mark on every physical artifact.
money_angle: Physical IP: a subscription archive that mails one letterpress-stamped, hand-numbered DEED certificate per month (edition of 250), each recording a fictional parcel of the vanishing town with vermilion seal and wax. Tiers: the monthly Deed drop, annual bound Ledger volumes (analog-premium monograph), and licensable seal/typography system for set-dressing and title sequences. The stamp itself becomes a sold object (custom brass DEED OFFICE stamp + vermilion pad kit).
what_makes_it_sellable: It converts the cheapest possible thing (a government form) into a scarce, hand-numbered, wax-sealed object you can hold. Per the analog-premium thesis, digital makes the physical certificate MORE valuable, not less. Per status psychology, owning Deed No. 014 of 250 is a quiet costly-signal of taste, and the bureaucratic-sublime aesthetic is instantly legible and screenshot-friendly. The single vermilion discipline makes every post recognizable in one second.
what_could_make_it_huge: A continuity engine: the town has a finite, knowable number of parcels, so the archive has a built-in ending (the last deed ever filed), which creates collector urgency and a narrative arc fans follow for years. Title-sequence and production-design licensing (the seal, the room, the typography) opens a B2B film/TV revenue lane on top of the consumer archive.
what_could_kill_it: If it drifts into generic 'vintage paper aesthetic' it dies, the whole moat is the institutional specificity and the strict one-red rule. Over-rendering the Clerk's face (breaking faceless-safe) or letting other colors creep in collapses the discipline. If the certificates feel like print-on-demand junk instead of genuinely letterpressed and numbered, the analog premium evaporates.
hero_prompts: A dead-on eye-level photograph inside a closing county Hall of Records, late afternoon. A municipal oak counter with a brass rail fills the lower third of the frame. Two anonymous hands in a grey wool cardigan with sleeve garters press a heavy brass date-stamp down onto a thick paper deed certificate, leaving a wet vermilion circular seal with a horizontal date-bar dead center of the document. No face is visible, only forearms and the crown of a bent head out of focus at the top edge. Behind: floor-to-ceiling oak index-card drawers labeled A through Z, frosted-glass partition, single bank of cold fluorescent tubes. Entire scene is desaturated grey-green and oak-brown EXCEPT the vermilion ink, which is the only saturated color in frame. Bureaucratic symmetry, shallow depth of field on the seal, fine paper grain, faint dust in the light. Editorial restraint, archival, quiet, no people performing.

A low clerk's-eye-level photograph looking down the aisle of THE STACKS: two facing walls of antique oak index drawers receding to a sealed vault door at the vanishing point. In the foreground on a rolling library ladder rung rests a single half-open drawer holding numbered deed certificates, each marked with a small round vermilion stamp (a circle with one horizontal bar). A single anonymous hand, ink-stained right index finger, half-moon reading glasses laid on the drawer edge, never worn. The world is monochrome municipal grey-green and brown under failing fluorescent light, EXCEPT every stamp seal which glows saturated vermilion, the only color allowed. Deep one-point perspective, symmetrical, dust motes, faint paper smell implied through texture, no face anywhere, contemplative and severe.
